newsitem.title: INDIA: Ganges river control irritant in Bangladesh ties.
newsitem.headline: Ganges river control irritant in Bangladesh ties.

text.p: The Ganges river has been a major irritant in India's relations with neighbouring Bangladesh, which accuses New Delhi of alternately releasing too much or too little of water from the river.

The decades-old water dispute worsened after India built its Farakka Barrage in 1974, restricting the flow of the Ganges, which irrigates a sprawling area of northern India before emptying into the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh.
Dhaka says the barrage, 18 km (11 miles) from Bangladesh's border, leaves 40 million people exposed to desertification by holding back water in the dry January-June period.
It says India then causes flooding in the monsoon season by releasing too much water from the Ganges, which Hindus consider holy.
The Ganges dispute is seen as an acid test for Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was in the Indian capital on Wednesday for talks over water-sharing.
Officials said the two sides expected to reach an agreement before Hasina was to depart on Thursday.

The Ganges dispute has been a major thorn in the relationship that gradually soured after the heady days of 1971 when India fought a war with Pakistan to help in the formation of independent Bangladesh from East Pakistan.

The two nations signed an agreement in 1977 to let Bangladesh take a guaranteed minimum of 34,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs) between October and June every year. But the guarantee was dropped in a new six-year accord signed in 1982.

In 1995, then-prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) said her nation faced a crisis after the flow dipped to only 9,000 cusecs, leading to a lowering of the water table in the Ganges delta.

Khaleda has accused Hasina of being pro-India. The Ganges dispute is seen as critical for Hasina in her effort to consolidate the political future of her Awami League party which regained power in elections this year after 21 years.
Dhaka said a draft water-sharing agreement was prepared during a recent visit to Bangladesh by Jyoti Basu, the powerful communist chief minister of India's West Bengal state.
The state neighbours Bangladesh and also needs huge amounts of Ganges water for its Calcutta port.
